title: Two Kinds of Text
goal: String owns and grows; &str borrows and views; methods flow between them.

sections.text: Rust has two everyday text types, and every confusing string error comes from mixing them up. `String` owns its text and can grow. `&str` is borrowed text: a view of characters that live somewhere else. Every literal in your source, like `"ferris"`, is a `&str`.

sections.code:
let borrowed: &str = "ferris";
let owned: String = String::from("ferris");
sections.caption: Same characters, different relationships to them.

sections.text: The working rule: functions that only read text take `&str`, and functions that produce new text return `String`. A literal passes straight into a `&str` parameter. A `String` does not - but `&owned` does, through a conversion the Core decks explain properly.

Methods move between the two types, and chains type-check one step at a time. `trim()` returns a `&str` view of the same text. `to_string()`, `to_uppercase()`, and `replace(..)` allocate and return an owned `String`. The order of a chain decides its type.

sections.code:
let cleaned = raw.trim();            // &str view
let owned = cleaned.to_string();     // owned String
sections.caption: trim borrows; to_string allocates.

sections.text: Growing text in place uses `push_str` on a `mut String`. The `+` operator also concatenates but consumes its left side - if that sounds strange, good: it is the door to the ownership decks, where it becomes obvious.

explanation: String owns and grows; &str borrows and views; methods flow between them.
